traps.why: E2 needs a β-hydrogen on the halide, and CH₃I has none. With a methyl halide SN2 is the only option; the alkoxide is the nucleophile, not a substrate for elimination.
CH₃I is an electrophile that gets attacked at carbon by the alkoxide oxygen; it is not a methyl nucleophile (that would be a Grignard).
Iodide is the leaving group, not a nucleophile here. The alkoxide oxygen attacks CH₃I.
NaH is a base, not an oxidant: it removes the O–H proton and nothing else.

nameTraps.name: cyclohexyl methoxide
nameTraps.why: '-oxide' names an anion. The ether is methoxycyclohexane or cyclohexyl methyl ether.

explanation: NaH deprotonates cyclohexanol to the alkoxide, which displaces iodide from CH₃I by SN2: methoxycyclohexane.
tip: Base first to make the alkoxide, then the methyl halide.

flaws.why: Step 1 (NaOH) does nothing here: NaOH is too weak to deprotonate an ordinary alcohol fully; use NaH or Na to make the alkoxide.

Step 1 (CH₃I) does nothing here: A neutral alcohol does not attack an alkyl halide; make the alkoxide first (NaH or Na), then add the halide.
